ceramic.snippet:
Earlier this year, a team at HKUST released something the field needed badly: LOCA-bench — a benchmark that tests how agents degrade as c

 We ran four controlled experiment families totaling 1,296 unique row-backed solve runs. Every experiment has the same basic shape — a set of coding tasks graded three ways (correctness 0/1/2, hallucination 0/1/2, compilable 0/1) — with one variable changed at a time: context size (EXP1), retrieval quality (EXP2), distractor type (EXP3), or compression approach (EXP4). Everything ran at temperature 0. EXP1 covers all four flagship-tier models; EXP2 uses Opus and GPT-5.4; EXP3 and EXP4 use the three flagship-family models (Opus, Sonnet, GPT-5.4) with Gemini excluded per the brief.  Sample sizes: the 1,296 calls are distributed across (model × condition × size) cells, with per-cell n ranging from 16 to 45. Findings represent directional patterns across multiple conditions and cross-model consistency rather than fully certified single-cell effect sizes. Scoring was done by Claude Sonnet 4.6 as LLM-as-judge with 216 rows manually re-scored as a validation sample; we ran the judge on a different model than the three other flagship models under test to reduce — though not eliminate — same-model circularity. The aggregate inter-rater agreement metric specified in the judge prompt was not computed as a summary statistic in our data, so we do not report it; the 216 re-scored rows are available alongside the raw JSONL on request.  Three accuracy metrics appear in this article , defined in full in Appendix A:  strict full credit (correctness = 2) is used on chart Y-axes labelled “full credit”;  weighted correctness (mean(score) / 2 × 100) is the default for body-prose headline accuracy numbers;  at-least-partial (correctness ≥ 1) appears as a diagnostic where it reveals a correct-area-wrong-fix pattern (notably Gemini in EXP1). Hallucination rates throughout are reported as the share of responses scoring hallucination ≥ 1.

Learned embedding spaces are known to be anisotropic, with vectors concentrating in a narrow cone on the hypersphere (Gao et al., 2019; Ethayarajh, 2019). Align then Train: Efficient Retrieval Adapter Learning
Seiji Maekawa
Moin Aminnaseri
Pouya Pezeshkpour
Estevam Hruschka
Megagon Labs
{seiji,moin,pouya,estevam}@megagon.ai
Abstract
Dense retrieval systems increasingly need to handle complex queries. In
many realistic settings, users express intent through long instructions or
task-specific descriptions, while target documents remain relatively simple
and static. This asymmetry creates a retrieval mismatch: understanding
queries may require strong reasoning and instruction-following, whereas
efficient document indexing favors lightweight encoders. Existing retrieval
systems often address this mismatch by directly improving the embed-
ding model, but fine-tuning large embedding models to better follow such
instructions is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and oper-
ationally burdensome. To address this challenge, we propose Efficient
Retrieval Adapter (ERA), a label-efficient framework that trains retrieval
adapters in two stages: self-supervised alignment and supervised adap-
tation. Inspired by the pre-training and supervised fine-tuning stages of
LLMs, ERA first aligns the embedding spaces of a large query embedder
and a lightweight document embedder, and then uses limited labeled data
to adapt the query-side representation, bridging both the representation gap
between embedding models and the semantic gap between complex queries
and simple documents without re-indexing the corpus. Experiments on the
MAIR benchmark, spanning 126 retrieval tasks across 6 domains, show that
ERA improves retrieval in low-label settings, outperforms methods that
rely on larger amounts of labeled data, and effectively combines stronger
query embedders with weaker document embedders across domains.

Abstract: Text-based person anomaly search requires a model to retrieve individuals from a large image gallery using natural-language descriptions of both appearance and behavior. ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval

Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon

cs.IR, cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG

2026-11-20

ERA 用几千个锚点文档训练轻量投影层,让新编码器的查询直接搜旧向量索引,免重嵌语料,五个 BEIR 基准上最多提升 35%。

## 这篇在解决什么

向量检索有个隐性锁定:索引是哪个嵌入模型建的,查询就得用同一个模型编码,换模型等于重嵌整个语料。很多时候这条路根本走不通:索引在第三方手里、原始文档拿不回来、语料还在持续入库。论文研究「跨模型潜空间检索」:查询用 A 模型编码,经一个投影层进 B 模型的索引直接检索。Embedding-Converter、LEAF、Drift-Adapter 等先前工作已证明这类映射可行,这篇卡的是部署第一天:冷启动,没有查询日志、没有标注,训练预算按锚点文档数计算,而投影注定在少数难查询上失手,恰好这些查询最影响用户对检索质量的感知。

## 方法

ERA 分三步。

- Embed,选锚点:用 Cosine Farthest Point Sampling(余弦最远点采样)从目标索引里挑锚点文档,每轮选与已选集合余弦相似度最低的那个。真实语料高度冗余,均匀采样会把小预算花在近重复文档上;最远点采样先覆盖目标空间的不同区域。挑选只用索引里现成的向量,真实成本在于把选中锚点用源模型再嵌一遍。
- Adapt,训适配器:两层 SwiGLU MLP,隐藏维 4096,损失是逐样本余弦对齐加 Global Orthogonal Regularization(惩罚批内投影向量两两的余弦相关)。正交项防的是表示坍缩:锚点一少,逐点回归为压低平均误差会把所有投影挤进超球面上的窄锥,近邻检索就没法区分文档。
- Route,难查询升级:轻量路由器预测源空间与目标空间 top-10 检索结果的重合度,低重合度标记投影大概率失手的查询;按预算对应的分位数定阈值,最差的一批交给目标模型编码。路由器跑在独立的开源小编码器上,与源模型解耦,升级的查询不用付两次 API 费用。

冷启动默认 4000 个锚点,单块 TPUv3 十分钟内训完;之后随无标注查询积累,还有域内微调和跨域 Foundation 两个阶段继续提升,全程零标注。

## 结果

主对照(text-embedding-004 → gemini-embedding-001,纯适配器,0% 路由):

|   |   |   |   |
| - | - | - | - |
| 方法 | ArguAna nDCG@10 | FiQA nDCG@10 | NFCorpus nDCG@10 |
| LEAF(逐点 L2 回归) | 0.340 | 0.424 | 0.230 |
| ERA | 0.459 | 0.475 | 0.243 |

相对提升 ArguAna +35%、FiQA +11.8%;衡量投影对目标空间保真度的 T-nDCG@10 在五个 BEIR 数据集上全部超过 LEAF。消融显示两项损失缺一不可:去掉余弦对齐,FiQA 的 T-nDCG@10 从 0.604 掉到 0.494;去掉正交项,ArguAna 的 nDCG@10 从 0.459 掉到 0.377。

锚点选择独立于损失函数起效:400 个锚点时把均匀采样换成 FPS,ERA 在 ArguAna 的 T-nDCG@10 从 0.361 升到 0.568,连 Embedding-Converter 也从 0.173 升到 0.413;锚点过几千后收益递减,不需要全库。

20% 升级预算下,路由器在 SciFact 抓到 37.5% 的 Huge-Gap 查询(同量级随机分配为 0%),SciDocs 上 32.0% 对 8.0%;随机策略有 15.9% 的概率错过 SciFact 全部 8 条 Huge-Gap 查询,约六次部署踩一次。适配器加路由只添 1.2ms,本地 Qwen-0.6B 约 20ms,端到端 37.7–85.5ms,而每条查询都调 Gemini API 要 160ms 以上。跨 API 配置里 SciFact 在 20% 预算下做到 0.868,原生 Gemini 是 0.916。

###### Abstract

Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. ultimate.snippet:
Align then Train: Efficient Retrieval Adapter Learning
Seiji Maekawa
Moin Aminnaseri
Pouya Pezeshkpour
Estevam Hruschka
Megagon Labs
{seiji,moin,pouya,estevam}@megagon.ai
Abstract
Dense retrieval systems increasingly need to handle complex queries. In
many realistic settings, users express intent through long instructions or
task-specific descriptions, while target documents remain relatively simple
and static. This asymmetry creates a retrieval mismatch: understanding
queries may require strong reasoning and instruction-following, whereas
efficient document indexing favors lightweight encoders. Existing retrieval
systems often address this mismatch by directly improving the embed-
ding model, but fine-tuning large embedding models to better follow such
instructions is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and oper-
ationally burdensome. To address this challenge, we propose Efficient
Retrieval Adapter (ERA), a label-efficient framework that trains retrieval
adapters in two stages: self-supervised alignment and supervised adap-
tation. Inspired by the pre-training and supervised fine-tuning stages of
LLMs, ERA first aligns the embedding spaces of a large query embedder
and a lightweight document embedder, and then uses limited labeled data
to adapt the query-side representation, bridging both the representation gap
between embedding models and the semantic gap between complex queries
and simple documents without re-indexing the corpus. Experiments on the
MAIR benchmark, spanning 126 retrieval tasks across 6 domains, show that
ERA improves retrieval in low-label settings, outperforms methods that
rely on larger amounts of labeled data, and effectively combines stronger
query embedders with weaker document embedders across domains.
